turn_text: This is Radio Works, Director of News and Information, Justine Whetrick. Today on the phone we are talking to U.S. Senator Tina Smith, who has just introduced some new legislation regarding atomic veterans. Thanks for joining us today, Senator.
Well, thank you, Justine, and I am glad to be able to talk about this. There are so many Minnesotans who are veterans or who have family members that are veterans. just like you, I believe, so

that is a really important issue. I'm a little confused because I'm looking at the legislation that you have introduced and I'm looking at the Radiation Exposure Compensation Act that came out in 1990. So how did that not include some of these veterans that helped clean up the Marshall Islands in the 70s?

Well, it was just a loophole that got left open and needs to be closed. You know, what the situation is, as you say, is there were all of these nuclear tests on the Marshall Islands from the late 1940s through the 1950s. And then when that testing was done, U.S. service people went on to the Marshall Islands and in shorts and t-shirts and combat boots, cleaned up the radioactive debris, exposing themselves to really dangerous radiation. And a lot of those folks today, through their lives, experienced increase cancers and respiratory illnesses. And so my bill would close that loophole and make sure that they get the same level of benefit and care that other service people who were involved in nuclear testing have gotten.
And these are gentlemen that we're not talking about like 70 and 80 year old men, we're talking about like ones in their fifties, right?

Yeah, people who are you know, many of these some of these some service people have have already been lost. And I just think it's a matter of principle, too, that people who risk their lives for this country, who serve our country, should expect to get the care and the respect that this bill is offering them. And the good news is that there is bipartisan support for this. I've introduced this with one of my Republican colleagues from North Carolina. And we've got lots of co-sponsors, which is a sign of support, but now we just have to get it over the finish line.
And would it kind of work the way the original act did that they'd be eligible for like a one time benefit or some monthly payments or is that what you're shooting for?

Yes, it would essentially make the same benefits that are available to veterans under the radiation compensation exposure act it would make these veterans who did the cleanup eligible for those same benefits
so what is the process now going forward you've introduced it now what happens well

now we have to you know the way a bill becomes a lot of it has to pass both the senate and the house and a piece of really good news is with the change in leadership in the united states house of representative their strong support for that and i have a high level of hope that we can get it passed through the House. And in the Senate, as I said, we've got bipartisan support. We just couldn't get the leadership to bring the bill up. I think if it had been brought up on the Senate floor, it would have passed overwhelmingly, if not unanimously. But we just couldn't get them to bring it up for a vote. So I'm going to be focused on getting a vote on this, either as a standalone bill, or maybe it could be rolled into another piece of legislation. that is going to be put up for a vote and get passed that way. So we'll look at all of our options.
Okay. And one question because we always have to ask this is where will the funding come from?

I would say that it's not a lot of money, which is a good thing. And I think that it can come out of the Veterans Administration and the Department of Defense where the funding for the existing benefits for atomic veterans comes from. And I think it's a question of a principle that we ought to Make sure that these veterans who served us that we serve them now.
If somebody is looking for more information about this, whether it's the current act or the legislation that you have put forward, what is the best way for them to find out more about that?

Well, the best thing for them to do would be to go onto my United States Senate website and find out information. And I also just Google Senator Tina Smith and it'll pop right up. And the other thing I want to say is a thank you to the many Veterans Service Organizations in Minnesota and around the country that have been working on this for a long time, and it brought this to our attention, and it's also been helping to push this. So I bet that if you went into the American Legion or some of those Veterans Service Organizations, they'd also have information about this bill.
All right. Well, is there anything else that you wanted to add today, Senator?

I just want to hope that everyone takes care and I know this weather has been so challenging and if I want to say especially to Minnesota farmers, dairy farmers and others that if you've had any damages as a result of this storm don't hesitate to go and contact your local FSA office because you might be eligible for a low-interest loan to help do repairs, and don't hesitate to reach out now for help if you need it.
All right. Well, thanks for that information. We appreciate your time, and hopefully we'll talk to you again soon. All right. Thank you, Jeff Dean. Thanks.
